https://www.politico.eu/article/ceuta-cr.text: BRUSSELS — The political reaction to the surge of migrants into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta laid bare how sharply Europe’s migration debate has shifted, and how it’s forcing migrant-rights groups to rethink the way they make their case. Where previous migration crises often divided European leaders between calls for solidarity and demands for tougher controls, the response to Ceuta — where more than 100 people died last month as they tried to enter — was strikingly uniform. From the far right to the center left, political leaders overwhelmingly called for stronger borders and more effective deterrence. Advertisement Advertisement “The conversation around migration and the language used to refer to migrants has changed in many EU countries, even center-left member states,” said Michele LeVoy, director of the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants, a network of organizations that advocate for unauthorized migrants across Europe. In response, migrant-rights groups are changing tactics. As humanitarian appeals lose political traction, they are turning more heavily to the courts, building broader alliances and experimenting with new ways to talk about migration. “We’re trying to be stronger together by working with organizations from across civil society, working with lawyers to challenge litigation, and really showing that these policies are bad for everyone, not just migrants,” LeVoy added. From rescue to deterrence In 2013, the death of hundreds of migrants in a shipwreck off the Italian island of Lampedusa shocked the continent. Top EU officials, including then-Commission President José Manuel Barroso, traveled to the site to declare that “the European Union cannot accept that thousands of people die at its borders.” The bloc’s then-Home Affairs Commissioner Cecilia Malmström called for a “change of approach towards migration,” adding that “this restrictive approach is not sustainable and that it is now time to move towards more openness and solidarity.” Advertisement Advertisement The 2015 refugee crisis initially generated a similarly humanitarian reaction, with German Chancellor Angela Merkel calling on Europeans to welcome more than 1 million people fleeing war in Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq. The European Commission sought to manage the crisis through measures including the redistribution of asylum seekers among EU countries. But that approach ran into resistance from figures like then-Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Poland’s Law and Justice party. Florian Trauner, an expert on EU migration at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel and the College of Europe, said a handful of right-wing politicians succeeded in establishing an “institutional deadlock” that halted EU efforts to integrate migrants and allowed for a “wider shift to a more restrictive, control-oriented approach to migration.” José Manuel Barroso attends a press conference at Lampedusa Airport on Oct. 9, 2013. | Tullio M. Puglia/Getty Images That evolution is visible in the EU’s response to Ceuta. Center-left figures like Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen echoed right-wing Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s call for a more robust defense of the bloc’s external borders, and twenty-two EU leaders signed onto a letter demanding a coordinated effort to “deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration.” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen likewise stressed that “control of our European borders matters.” Without mentioning the rising death toll, she instead celebrated the fact that “not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of the EU.” The far-right factor The bloc’s shift on migration has been accelerated by the rise of far-right parties and a scramble by centrist rivals to neutralize them by embracing parts of their agenda. Advertisement Advertisement “The buffer zone that once separated the democratic right from the far right has effectively disappeared,” said Estrella Galán, a European Parliament lawmaker with the far-left Left group who is the shadow rapporteur on the EU’s return regulation. As hard-line positions have gone mainstream, the far-right has started to push for further measures, including “remigration” — the removal of immigrants from Europe. “As their policies have become widely accepted, the far-right groups have moved further and further right on other issues,” said Trauner. Hungarian border police officiers patrol the Hungarian-Serbian border on Dec. 15, 2022. | Attila Kisbenedek/AFP via Getty Images The Trump administration’s approach to migration — including large-scale deportations — “has given legitimacy to European actors who have been able to reject criticism by pointing out that the world’s major international power is embracing the exact same position,” Trauner said. Helena Maleno, spokesperson for Caminando Fronteras, an NGO that defends migrants’ rights along the western Euro-African border, said her group was increasingly being targeted by the far right. “There is a total dehumanization of migrants, especially if they’re Muslims,” she said. “We have had to reinforce protection and security — from digital attacks, but also from threats to our physical safety.” Advertisement Advertisement The far right, however, argues that migrant-rights groups have not lost influence — and still have too much of it. “I wish we could speak of the failure of pro-immigration NGOs, but what happened in Ceuta proves they have not failed,” said Jorge Buxadé, a European Parliament lawmaker from Spain’s Vox party. He accused migrants’ rights groups of being “21st-century pirates” who use “hybrid warfare” to undermine Spain’s territorial integrity. A Polish border guard stands at the Polish-Belarusian border on July 21, 2025. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images “Billions of euros every year go toward funding the structure and influence of organizations whose sole interest is ensuring that immigration to Europe remains massive and uncontrolled,” he said. Change in tactics In the new climate, the humanitarian argument traditionally used by rights groups — that migrants are human beings in need of protection — no longer carries the same political weight, said LeVoy. Increasingly, NGOs have found themselves on the defensive, fighting criminal sanctions and restrictions on their activities rather than shaping the broader debate. Advertisement Advertisement That pressure is pushing migrant-rights groups to rethink where — and how — they fight. One response is to take the battle into the courts, investing resources in legal challenges to restrictive legislation, including EU rules governing returns and the criminalization of assistance to undocumented migrants. Migrant-rights groups are also seeking to broaden their alliances. In Spain, the recent push to grant legal status to hundreds of thousands of unauthorized migrants was backed by support from the country’s conservative employers’ association and the Catholic Church . Migrants from various detention centers across Italy are escorted by police upon arrival in Shëngjin, Albania on April 11, 2025. | Adnan Beci/AFP via Getty Images “It’s more important than ever to be in strong coalitions,” LeVoy said. Her group is also reaching out to local authorities, health professionals and housing organizations. LeVoy advocated for shifting the narrative on migration by focusing less on dangerous sea crossings or dramatic border surges. Instead, she argued, rights groups should highlight the much larger population of unauthorized migrants already living alongside Europeans. She likened the strategy to that of successful campaigns for marriage equality , which sought to change public perceptions by presenting LGBTQ+ people not as an abstract political constituency but as friends, colleagues and neighbors. Advertisement “Borders are really a very small part of this issue, because the overwhelming majority [of Europe’s unauthorized migrants] come in regularly,” LeVoy said. Caminando Fronteras has likewise reinforced its legal work and security measures and built transnational networks with other rights groups. But Maleno said her NGO was also staying true to its long-standing commitment to amplify the voices of families whose relatives have died or disappeared at Europe’s borders. “We will continue to work to make the public administrations listen,” she said. “Europe will one day have to account for all those deaths and disappearances.”

CCO-T shareholders are expected to share in the company’s massive win on an investment in Westinghouse Electric Co., with the Saskatoon-based uranium miner poised to boost dividends after a planned Westinghouse initial public offering. Pittsburgh-based Westinghouse, one of the world’s leading nuclear reactor manufacturers, is moving forward on an IPO this fall that analysts estimate will value the company at between US$30-billion and US$50-billion. Westinghouse is going public as global demand for nuclear power soars. In July, the company reported utilities around the world have ordered up to 91 of its flagship Advanced Passive 1000 reactors, known as the AP1000, for delivery over the next two decades. The stock market debut and premium valuation will mean major gains for joint owners Brookfield Renewable Partners and Cameco, which acquired Westinghouse in 2023 for US$8.3-billion, including assumed debt. Chris Cassin: Nuclear reactors produce one byproduct that is key to our future. Canada must stockpile it In late July, the two owners announced plans to list Westinghouse on a U.S. stock exchange. The company hired at least five investment banks to lead the offering, Bloomberg reported on Friday. Brookfield Renewable, a subsidiary of Brookfield Corp., owns a 51-per-cent stake in Westinghouse and Cameco holds 49 per cent. Westinghouse had filed for bankruptcy before Brookfield’s private equity arm bought the company from Toshiba Corp. for US$4.6-billion in 2018. If Westinghouse does go public, analysts say Cameco is expected to return part of the proceeds from any sale of its stake to shareholders, by raising its common stock dividend. Cameco doubled its common stock dividend between 2023 and 2025, boosting the payout from 12 cents per share to 24 cents. The increase came a year ahead of the company’s target. Cameco’s board of directors said it raised dividends in part because Westinghouse made its first cash payment to its owners in 2025, with the miner receiving US$220.5-million. Early this year, Westinghouse handed an additional US$49-million to Cameco. “We anticipate further improvements to dividends ahead,” said analyst Orest Wowkodaw at Bank of Nova Scotia in a recent report. He projected Westinghouse’s reactor sales and Cameco’s rising uranium production will result in a fivefold increase in the mining company’s free cash flow, to $1.3-billion in 2028. Brookfield Renewable is also expected to benefit from Westinghouse’s public market debut. In a report, analyst Nelson Ng at RBC Capital Markets said the company will “benefit from growing demand for carbon-free baseload generation and potential valuation uplift from an IPO.” Westinghouse is going public with orders for 22 AP1000 reactors from U.S. clients, including two units earmarked for the restart of the V.C. Summer power plant in South Carolina, a Brookfield-led project. The company has also sold seven of the reactors to customers in Poland, Bulgaria and Ukraine. “Timelines and valuation remain uncertain at this point, but we do recognize the potential for a significant valuation should the stated new build pipeline materialize in the 2030s,” mining analyst Katie Lachapelle at Canaccord Genuity Capital Markets said in a report. She predicted an “uplift” in Cameco’s stock price as more details emerge on Westinghouse’s IPO plans. Westinghouse is also rolling out new power plant technology, including small modular reactors and micro reactors. In a report on Cameco, analyst Andrew Wong at RBC Capital Markets said the development costs on these projects are “relatively moderate” at roughly US$1.2-billion. “We view Westinghouse as a unique asset with no direct publicly-traded peer which justifies a premium valuation,” Mr. Wong said. Since Mr. Wong published his report, RBC Capital Markets has placed Cameco on what is known as a restricted list and stopped releasing research reports, a common move when an investment bank is doing corporate finance work for a client, such as advising on an IPO. Westinghouse selected Wall Street banks Citigroup Inc. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to lead its IPO, along with JPMorgan Chase & Co. and the investment banking arms of Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and Royal Bank of Canada, according to media reports. https://www.dw.com/en/iran-balances-ties.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PaQi Prefer DW on Google China and Russia back Iran but must balance that support against broader interests with Washington Image: Mandel Ngan/AFP Advertisement As Donald Trump , Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support. For Iran , relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow. Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran . But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington. That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate? Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video China is now Iran's economic lifeline China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil. In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports , much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions. As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs. Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, says China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own. "If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW. But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter. "The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost said. Sanctions enforcement raises pressure on Iran That distinction has become more important as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports. In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny. As a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets. "A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said. Iran prepares for the worst This economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning. A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently said the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero. That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks. Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating. What does Beijing want? Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost. But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies. A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping . China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability. Russia can help, but how much? Russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation. Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify. Trump, Xi and Putin each seek to advance competing interests on Iran, Ukraine, trade and international security Image: Sergey Bobylev/SNA/IMAGO Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, believes the summit should be viewed within a larger attempt to manage the wars in both Ukraine and the Middle East . "Russia, China and the United States appear to be seeking constructive dialogue and results that could shape a new security architecture in the international system," Vakhshiteh told DW. Russia supports Iran, but limits remain Solhdoost also warns against overstating Russian support for Iran. The strategic partnership between Moscow and Tehran provides for security cooperation and efforts to counter unilateral sanctions, but it does not require Russia to enter a war on Iran's behalf. Since Russia is deeply engaged in Ukraine, it likely has its own priorities in negotiations with Washington, says Solhdoost. "Russia would prioritize its own national interests in negotiations with the US over Ukraine and Iran," he said. Moscow could support Iran while simultaneously using its relationship with Tehran as leverage in talks with Trump over Ukraine. How much influence do the three powers have? For Iran, ties with China and Russia remain essential. They provide alternative trade routes, export markets and diplomatic support that complicate Washington's efforts to isolate Tehran. Yet neither Beijing nor Moscow views Iran solely through the lens of strategic partnership. Both weigh support for Tehran against their own economic interests, security concerns and dealings with Washington. Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
